summary: Lithuania is the largest of the three Baltic states. In the Middle Ages the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was one of the largest states in Europe, and in 1990 Lithuania was the first to declare independence from the Soviet Union.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1387 Grand Duke Jogaila led Lithuania's conversion to Catholicism in order to unite with Poland, and from then on Catholicism became closely tied to the culture of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. During Russian imperial and Soviet rule, the Catholic Church became a force preserving the Lithuanian language and national identity, and in the 1980s the Church also supported the independence movement, so it remains the faith of the great majority to this day.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: During 50 years of Soviet rule, atheist education was promoted, churches were closed and clergy persecuted, leaving some people with no religious affiliation. However, compared with neighboring Estonia and Latvia, Catholic identity is stronger in Lithuania, and the proportion of people with no religion is relatively low.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodox believers are mainly Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians, mostly descendants of immigrants who arrived during the period of Russian imperial rule in the 19th century and the Soviet period, concentrated in Vilnius and industrial cities such as Visaginas in the east.

ranking.name: Old Believers
ranking.description: The Old Believers were followers who in the 17th century rejected the liturgical reforms of Patriarch Nikon of the Russian Orthodox Church; to escape persecution by the Russian government they moved to the Lithuanian lands, then part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. They preserve distinctive traditional rites, and a few communities still exist today.

religion.background: Lithuania was the last country in Europe to accept Christianity. In the 13th century Mindaugas was briefly baptized, but the Grand Duchy long maintained Baltic polytheism and fought long wars with the Teutonic Order. In 1387 Grand Duke Jogaila (Władysław II Jagiełło) united with Poland in order to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and Lithuania formally converted to Catholicism. In the 16th century the Reformation briefly influenced the nobility, but the Jesuits reconsolidated Catholicism during the Counter-Reformation. From 1795 it came under Russian imperial rule, the Orthodox Church expanded, and Catholicism became a symbol of resistance to Russification. During the Soviet period (1940–1990) religion was suppressed, and the Catholic underground publication of 1972 and the Hill of Crosses became symbols of resistance.

ranking.name: Lithuanian
ranking.description: Lithuanian is the language of the Lithuanian nation. During the Russian Empire's press ban (1864–1904) it was preserved by book smugglers and underground schools, and it became the core of the 19th-century national revival. Lithuanian was the national language in both independences of 1918 and 1990, and since ethnic Lithuanians make up more than 80 percent of the population, most people speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian was the dominant language of administration and education under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, and during the Soviet period large numbers of Russians moved into industrial cities such as Vilnius and Klaipėda. After independence in 1990 the status of Russian declined, but many Lithuanians of middle age and older still speak Russian, and the Russian-speaking community is concentrated in cities.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: Polish speakers mainly live in the area around Vilnius. This region was occupied by Poland in 1920–1939, and in the interwar period most residents of Vilnius were Poles and Jews; after World War II many Poles were resettled to Poland, but a large Polish community remains in the countryside, with its own schools and political party.

language.history: Lithuanian belongs to the Baltic branch of the Indo-European language family. Together with Latvian it is one of only two surviving Baltic languages, and linguists value it highly because it preserves many archaic Indo-European features. The written languages of the medieval Grand Duchy of Lithuania were in fact Old Church Slavonic, Latin and Polish, and the first Lithuanian book was published only in 1547. From 1864 to 1904 the Russian Empire banned the printing of Lithuanian books in the Latin alphabet, and Lithuanians preserved their language by smuggling books in from East Prussia through "book smugglers". After independence in 1918 Lithuanian became the national language; during the Soviet period the influence of Russian grew, and after independence in 1990 Lithuanian again became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Cepelinai (Zeppelin dumplings)
ranking.description: Large oval dumplings with a dough of raw grated potato mixed with cooked potato, filled with minced meat or cheese and boiled, topped with sour cream and diced bacon.
ranking.history: Cepelinai are named for their resemblance to German Zeppelin airships, a name that appeared only in the early 20th century. Potatoes became common in Lithuania only in the 18th–19th centuries, gradually replacing traditional grains as the staple, and cepelinai are representative of potato culture. Regarded as Lithuania's national dish, they take time to make and are often made collectively by families on weekends and holidays.

ranking.name: Šaltibarščiai (cold beet soup)
ranking.description: A bright pink cold soup made from pickled beets, cucumbers, dill and boiled eggs with fermented milk (kefir), eaten with hot potatoes.
ranking.history: Cold beet soup is Lithuania's representative summer dish, rooted in the Eastern European tradition of cooking soup with beets, with the addition of fermented dairy being a Lithuanian specialty. In the heat of summer people drink the cold soup to cool off, served with steaming boiled potatoes. In recent years Vilnius has even held a "Pink Soup Festival", and cold beet soup has become a cultural symbol that young Lithuanians are proud of.

ranking.name: Kibinai
ranking.description: Half-moon-shaped pies made of pastry dough filled with lamb, beef or chicken and onion, and baked. The crust is crisp and the filling juicy, and it is the signature snack of Trakai.
ranking.history: Kibinai is a traditional food of the Karaims, a Turkic people who follow Karaite Judaism, whom Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania brought from Crimea to Trakai in the late 14th century to serve as castle guards. They brought this pie to Lithuania, and to this day Trakai is the most famous place to taste kibinai, which is also a witness to Lithuania's multiethnic history.

ranking.name: Kugelis (potato pudding)
ranking.description: A thick pudding-like dish made by mixing mashed potatoes with bacon, onion and egg and baking it, served with sour cream. It has a browned, fragrant crust and a soft interior, with a rich and filling taste.
ranking.history: The name kugelis probably comes from the Yiddish or German kugel (pudding), reflecting the influence of Eastern European Jewish and German cuisine on Lithuania. After potatoes became common in the 19th century, kugelis became a cheap and filling dish for farm families, slowly baked in an oven for several hours. Today it is a common dish at Sunday family dinners and festivals, and it also became popular in Lithuanian communities in the United States with Lithuanian emigrants.

ranking.name: Šakotis (tree cake)
ranking.description: Batter is poured layer by layer onto a rotating wooden rod and baked over a fire into a tree-shaped cake with many spikes; when cut, it shows patterns like tree rings.
ranking.history: Šakotis is related to the German Baumkuchen, and the method of making it spread between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and neighboring regions. Folk legend says it originated at the court of Queen Bona in the 16th century, but there is no firm evidence. Making it requires a lot of eggs and butter; in the past it was a festive treat for wealthy families, and today it is the representative cake for Lithuanian weddings, birthdays and Christmas.
